what_it_does: Modern cars use an internal communication network called the CAN bus (Controller Area Network) to let components like the engine, brakes, and steering talk to each other. This paper presents a method to reverse-engineer exactly which individual bits (the smallest unit of digital data) in each CAN message correspond to which physical actions in the car — for example, which bit toggles the door lock. Getting this fine-grained mapping is hard because there are enormous numbers of possible message-and-payload combinations to search through. The authors built a systematic framework that exhaustively tests bit-level combinations and confirmed it on real vehicles (a Tesla Model 3 and two Leapmotor models). The tool is lightweight enough to run on a cheap Raspberry Pi, making it practical for security researchers who need to assess vulnerabilities in a car's network without expensive lab equipment.
